summary: Describes the architecture of WHOIS++, an extension of the simple WHOIS service in RFC 954 that lets WHOIS-like servers offer more structured information. It was standards-track but is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to link many small lookup services into one network so you can ask any of them anything.

subtitle: A structured, distributed directory service for finding information about people and resources on the Internet.

tldr.problem: The simple WHOIS service worked for small, centralized databases but could not scale to a distributed, Internet-wide directory. It lacked structure, rich query capabilities, and a way to locate information across multiple servers.
tldr.mechanism: WHOIS++ adds structured templates to organize information, an indexing service to interconnect multiple servers, and a query language with boolean operators and advanced search constraints.
tldr.outcome: WHOIS++ became Historic as web-based search and DNS-based directory services proved more practical for Internet-scale information discovery.

today: RFC 1835 is Historic. WHOIS++ was designed to scale the simple WHOIS service into a distributed, structured directory but did not achieve widespread adoption. Web-based search engines and DNS-based information discovery proved more practical and easier to implement at Internet scale.

sections.title: The Limits of Simple WHOIS
sections.content:
The original WHOIS service, defined in RFC 954, was a simple, unstructured lookup system for finding information about Internet users and domains. Each record consisted of text fields with no defined structure, and searches were limited to simple string matching within records.

As the Internet grew, organizations wanted to publish more kinds of information—not just user data but also service descriptions, abstracts, and organizational details. However, the simple WHOIS model could not accommodate this variety without becoming chaotic. WHOIS++ extends the original design with structured data templates, allowing different types of records to coexist with well-defined fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The old WHOIS was like a notebook where everyone scribbled whatever they wanted. WHOIS++ is like having proper forms where each kind of information gets filled in the same way every time.

sections.title: Templates, Records, and Distributed Indexing
sections.content:
WHOIS++ organizes information using templates: standardized forms that define a set of named attributes (like Name, Email, Organization). Each record belongs to a template type and contains values for those attributes. A WHOIS++ database contains multiple record types, each with its own template, all identified by a unique server handle registered with IANA.

The distributed architecture uses two types of servers. Base level servers contain the actual records. Index servers do not store records themselves; instead, they collect centroids—summaries of what each base server contains—allowing them to route queries to the right servers. Multiple index servers can be organized hierarchically, creating a searchable Internet-wide directory without requiring a single centralized database.
sections.plainLanguage: A base server is a library with books. An index server is a librarian who knows which libraries have which topics. The librarian reads a summary from each library and uses that to answer your questions.

sections.title: Searching and Constraints
sections.content:
A WHOIS++ search command specifies one or more search terms (values, attribute names, handles, or template types) and can combine them with boolean operators (AND, OR, NOT) and parentheses. For example, a user can search for records where the attribute Author equals Chris AND the template type is User. Each search term can apply a local constraint to affect how that term is matched.

WHOIS++ supports multiple search methods. The default exact method requires exact word matches, but servers can also support substring, lstring (leading string), regex (regular expressions), and fuzzy matching for names with different spelling. Global constraints like MAXHITS (maximum results), FORMAT (output format), and LANGUAGE (for multilingual support) apply to the entire search.
sections.plainLanguage: You can search for exact words, partial matches, or words that sound similar. You can combine searches with AND, OR, and NOT like a detective searching for clues. You can also tell the server how many results you want and what language to use.

sections.title: Flexible Output Formats and Extensibility
sections.content:
WHOIS++ servers respond in one of five formats depending on the client's needs. FULL format returns complete record details, ABRIDGED returns relevant highlights, HANDLE returns just the record identifiers, and SUMMARY returns a count of matches and matching template types. The optional SERVER-TO-ASK format tells the client which other servers might have the answer.

The architecture is designed for extensibility. Servers can define custom templates beyond the standard ones, implement different search engines (databases, gateways to other services), and support optional constraints like authentication, character set selection, and attribute filtering. The simple text-based protocol remains machine-parseable while remaining readable by humans, lowering the barrier to implementation and experimentation.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask for the full details, just a summary, or just the record names. Servers can add their own types of information and search methods without breaking the system.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
WHOIS++ includes optional password-based authentication and a framework for other authentication schemes (prefixed with X- for experimental ones). However, the specification is explicit: authentication does not encrypt the password or information in transit. As with the original WHOIS, WHOIS++ is designed as a public information service, and strong security was not a primary goal.

The specification acknowledges the tension between privacy (hiding information from the public Internet) and utility (offering a global directory service). Communities or organizations implementing WHOIS++ must decide whether to expose information publicly, restrict it to authenticated users, or implement a hybrid approach. The RFC notes that security considerations beyond basic authentication are outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The system can ask for a password, but that password travels without hiding. It is up to each organization to decide whether to share information publicly or only with approved users.
